beats.text: In 1849, an enslaved man mailed himself to freedom.

overlays.hook: In 1849, an enslaved man *mailed himself* to *freedom.*

beats.text: He worked in a tobacco factory in Richmond, Virginia.
In 1848, his wife and three children were sold away to North Carolina.

visual.sub: his wife and children, sold away

beats.text: So Brown planned an escape inside a box.

visual.caption: His box, as drawn in his 1849 narrative

beats.text: On March 23, 1849, two helpers sealed him in a wooden crate, three feet long.

visual.caption: Narrative of Henry Box Brown, Boston, 1849

beats.text: It was marked: This side up with care.

visual.caption: The lid, drawn in William Still's 1872 book

beats.text: It went by wagon, train and steamboat to Philadelphia.
Workers turned it upside down. For miles, he rode on his head.
He stayed still and silent for more than a day.

visual.title: Over a day
visual.sub: inside a box three feet long

beats.text: In Philadelphia, abolitionists pried off the lid.

visual.caption: James Miller McKim, who received the box

beats.text: Brown climbed out alive, and sang a hymn.
From then on, the world called him Henry Box Brown.
But in 1850, a new Fugitive Slave Law put him at risk of capture.
So he sailed to England, and took his story on stage.
He turned a shipping crate into a road to freedom.

facts.claim: In 1849 Brown, enslaved, escaped by shipping himself in a box to Philadelphia.

facts.note: Birth year 1815 or 1816 (EV), 1815 (BRIT); lower third says c. 1815.

facts.claim: Worked in a tobacco factory in Richmond, Virginia.
In 1848 his wife Nancy and their three children were sold to an owner in North Carolina.
facts.note: Nancy was pregnant with a fourth child (EV, BRIT, PSU); script says three children.

facts.claim: On 23 March 1849 he was sealed into a wooden box about 3 ft long, 2 ft wide, 2.5 ft deep, by two helpers (James C. A. Smith and Samuel A. Smith).
The box was marked 'This side up with care.'
facts.note: The 1849 narrative's drawing reads 'Right side up with care'; Still (1872) and the 1851 narrative say 'This side up with care'.

facts.claim: It travelled by wagon, railroad and steamboat to Philadelphia.
facts.note: STILL: dray to Adams' Express, then overland express; EV: shipped by train.

facts.claim: The box was turned upside down; he rode on his head for a long stretch.
facts.note: STILL: 'on his head for miles'; EV: head-down for several hours; PSU: about an hour and a half in the worst position.

facts.claim: He stayed still and silent; the trip took 26–27 hours.
facts.note: 26 hours (STILL, EV), 27 (BRIT); script says 'more than a day'.

facts.claim: In Philadelphia, at the Anti-Slavery office, abolitionists including James Miller McKim opened the box.
He came out alive and sang a hymn (based on Psalm 40).
He became known as Henry 'Box' Brown.
After the 1850 Fugitive Slave Act he feared capture.
He sailed to England (October 1850) and toured with his panorama and stage shows.

notUsed: Quote 'How do you do, gentlemen?' (Still's account only): not used.
